chunks: LDO as a variable series resistor. The question: An LDO can often be modeled as a single passive component, what is this passive component?
You can think of an LDO as a variable resistor in series with the load. The pass transistor drops the extra voltage, so it behaves like a resistor of (V in-V out) over I out .
The feedback loop keeps adjusting that resistance so the output stays fixed. This simple picture tells you the heat, the efficiency, and what dropout means.
Imagine a dimmer knob in series with a lamp, and a robot that turns it automatically. If the supply rises, the robot turns the resistance up.
If the lamp draws more current, the robot turns the resistance down. The lamp always gets the same voltage.
The analogy has one limit: a real pass transistor cannot go below its smallest on-resistance, and that limit is dropout.
The large-signal LDO model. The control loop (not drawn) adjusts R pass so that V out stays at 3. 3 volts as the load or V in changes.
The heat dissipated in this one resistor is the entire efficiency story.
Series resistor: a resistor in line with the load that drops part of the voltage ("Ohm's law: V = IR"). R DS(on) : the lowest resistance of the pass transistor when fully on.
Dropout: the point where the resistance has hit that minimum and cannot go lower. Power loss: heat in the pass device, (V in-V out) times I out .
Load current: the current the circuit draws from the output.
Take 5 volts in, 3. 3 volts out, and a 0. 5 amps load. The pass device drops 5-3. 3 equals 1. 7 volts at 0. 5 amps, so it acts like 1. 7 over 0. 5 equals 3. 4 ohms.
At a light load of 0. 05 amps it acts like 34 ohms. The heat in the first case is 1. 7 times 0. 5 equals 0. 85 watts. The efficiency is 3.
3 over 5 equals 66 % either way, since the same current flows in and out. That is the whole idea.
The pass transistor drops V in-V out at the load current, so it looks like R equals (V in-V out) over I out , and the feedback loop keeps adjusting that value to hold the output constant.
